opus-5.5.text:
For me, fundraising has always been a means, not the work itself. The core work is building the product and figuring out whether we're actually solving a real problem for real people. Fundraising is what buys you the time and resources to do that well.

Early on, I made the mistake a lot of founders make. I treated a successful round almost like a milestone of progress, as if closing the money meant we'd achieved something. Then you realize nothing about the product changed the day the wire hit. The users didn't care. The hard problems were still sitting there waiting for you.

So now I try to think of it in a more disciplined way. First, how much runway do we really need to reach the next point where we've learned something meaningful, where the company is clearly different than it is today? You raise for that, with some buffer, because things always take longer than you think.

Second, I try to keep it contained in time. Fundraising can easily eat three or four months of a founder's attention if you let it. Your head is full of pitch meetings and term sheets, and the team can feel that you're not fully there. I'd rather run a focused process, get it done, and get back to the work.

And third, who you raise from matters more than the headline valuation. Investors become part of your life for many years. I care whether they understand what we're trying to do, whether they'll be patient when things are hard, and whether they'll be honest with me. A slightly higher price from someone who doesn't share your view of the long term can cost you a lot more later.

So in short, fundraising serves the mission. If it starts to feel like the mission, that's usually a sign something's off.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising supports product building and solving real problems, but does not identify the core work as advancing AGI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing aligned investors, but does not say investors proactively showed interest because of progress toward AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Chen Xie: Honestly, I try to keep fundraising in a very small box. It's a means, not the work. When we started, I had this idea that raising money was a milestone, something you celebrate. And after the first round I realized it's closer to buying time. You've sold a piece of the company in exchange for a few years of runway, and the question is just whether you use that time well.

So the way I think about it now is that fundraising should follow the product, not lead it. If we're raising, it's because there's a concrete thing we want to build or a market we want to enter, and we can explain clearly why it needs capital rather than just more patience. If I can't explain that in two sentences, we probably shouldn't be raising.

The other thing I've learned is that the fundraising process itself is a distraction for the team if you let it leak. So I try to absorb most of it myself and keep the engineers and researchers focused. The worst version is when the whole company starts optimizing for what investors want to hear, and the narrative gets ahead of the reality. You end up building the deck instead of the product.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive about it. The people you take money from matter a lot. A good investor gives you honest feedback, introductions, and room to be wrong for a while. A bad one makes every board meeting about the next round. So I spend real time on who, and as little time as possible on how much.

r001.rationale: The response describes fundraising as secondary to product work, but it does not identify the company’s core work as advancing AGI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing investors, but does not say their interest is driven by the company’s progress toward AGI.

astra-6.text: I think fundraising should serve the company’s core work. It gives you resources to build the product, bring in the right people, and learn from customers, but raising money isn’t itself proof that you’re creating value. I’d start with what we need to accomplish and then ask how much capital would help us get there. Otherwise, fundraising can become a distraction from the very business it’s supposed to support.
